title: Saying numbers out loud
subtitle: A chemical formula came out as a sneeze and a thousand as ten thousand; a speech contract and a deterministic scrubber give the voice speakable text while the screen keeps the written answer

stats.label: character ceiling on any clause, set by the synthesiser's own limits

lede: A reasoning model writes for a screen. It writes "H₂O", "8.832", "abcdef.md", "U.S." and "1000", and every one of those is a trap for a synthesiser that speaks phonemes. In real use the formula for water came out as a sneeze, a thousand was spoken as ten thousand, a filename was read as a word, and the abbreviation for the country became "u dot s". Each is small. Together they are the difference between an assistant that sounds like a colleague and one that sounds like a machine reading a document. The first layer is a speech contract in the prompt. The model follows it most of the time, and most of the time is not enough for speech.
quote: I pair a contract the model is asked to follow with a deterministic layer that does not rely on it following.
evidence: Speech synthesis pipelines: two layers between the model and the speaker, a prompt contract and a deterministic scrubber of about 800 lines on every clause.
Text normalisation for TTS: formulas, large numbers, paths and abbreviations rewritten only for the voice, while subtitles and history keep what the model wrote.
Property-based testing: every clause split checked to land on sentence-ending punctuation, under a 500-character ceiling.
author: Corey James
